title: Idea: inventory the entity's AI and scope it to financial reporting
problem: Idea, not a deployment: auditors cannot tell which AI touches financial reporting when entities use embedded features, vendor tools and unsanctioned shadow AI.
approach: Idea: keep a living inventory classifying each use case by COSO capability type, with an owner, and map it to key controls.
BDO starts the IT audit with the entity's AI use cases; EY leaders advise beginning with governance and an AI inventory.
Management signs off ownership and criticality, and agrees with auditors what evidence suffices.

title: Classify AI-enabled controls by reliance to set the evidence standard
problem: Some AI-assisted controls are re-performed by a person and others accepted on AI output alone, yet both are called AI controls, so evidence demands go too heavy or too light.
approach: COSO defines reliance as management depending on AI output as control evidence; reliance brings ICFR evidence standards, including prompt and model version.
BDO applies the test to IT general controls scoping; a finance-technology vendor sorts controls into three classes by the AI's role.
In non-reliance patterns the control owner re-performs and documents the review; the auditor decides which pattern applies.

title: Extend IT general controls to AI components; choose how to test them
problem: IT controls testing was built around applications and databases, but AI adds models, data pipelines and agents that can act on ERP systems.
approach: BDO extends the four IT control domains to in-scope AI components, scoped by reliance; COSO treats prompts as governed configurations.
The AICPA aid, as reported, says auditors may test AI outputs substantively, or test controls over data quality and model performance.
KPMG expects the first wave of AI-related material weaknesses in 2027 as programmes stop testing around AI (self-reported forecast).

title: Build an evidence trail for each AI-touched control, from prompts onward
problem: Because GenAI is probabilistic, a control relying on its output cannot be evidenced by the output alone, and agents that trigger side effects need reconstructable records.
approach: COSO says significant GenAI processes should keep an AI bill of materials logging prompts, outputs, model version and parameters.
A vendor adds a control-matrix crosswalk mapping each AI detection rule to the audit risk factor it addresses.
A named reviewer documents what the AI concluded and why they agreed or disagreed.

title: Idea: use management's AI monitoring metrics and remediation logs as audit evidence
problem: Idea, not a deployment: point-in-time testing misses gradual model drift and vendor-driven changes, so set-and-forget does not work for GenAI in financial reporting.
approach: COSO expects continuous monitoring of accuracy, coverage and exception volumes, separate evaluations, a remediation log and a deficiency playbook.
Deloitte lists transaction volume, size and override percentages as drift indicators and calls for root-cause review.
Control owners review drift alerts; material deficiencies escalate to governance bodies.

title: Idea: re-perform AI-operated control outputs with test populations or challenger models
problem: Idea, not a deployment: an auditor cannot inspect a probabilistic model's reasoning, so comfort over its output is harder to reach.
approach: COSO lists methods under discussion: full re-performance or risk-based sampling, performance testing on test populations, and multi-model validation against independent models.
Other methods include analytics monitoring of drift and third-party validation of models.
Human reviewers handle disagreements between the model and the challenger.

title: Idea: evidence over vendor-supplied AI through service-auditor reports and representations
problem: Idea, not a deployment: when an entity uses a service organisation's AI, the user auditor's ability to perform procedures may be limited.
approach: Idea: a service auditor's report becomes important evidence; if insufficient, add AI-related management representations such as identifying the AI the entity uses.
The AICPA aid also asks whether the entity has a process to identify vendor AI and evaluate its effect on financial reporting.
The user auditor checks the report covers the relevant AI controls.

title: Idea: extend fraud-risk assessment to AI manipulation and AI-generated evidence
problem: Idea, not a deployment: COSO says AI creates new fraud routes including deepfakes, synthetic records and model manipulation through crafted prompts.
approach: Idea: COSO Principle 8 asks fraud risk assessment to identify how these threats could be used and whether controls would catch them.
The AICPA aid, as reported, gives examples such as altering training data and generating fictitious supporting documents.
The engagement team's fraud-risk discussion covers AI-enabled schemes.

title: Audit committee oversight of AI reporting risk, via dialogue with the auditor
problem: Audit committees are taking on AI oversight faster than they feel able to carry it: 75% named it a top-three priority but only 56% felt confident.
approach: KPMG's Board Leadership Center tells committees to ask the auditor how the plan assesses risks from the company's GenAI and agents.
It also suggests tasking management to reassess whether disclosure controls support statements about AI use.
About two-thirds of audit partners say their committee raised AI use in the past 12 months (independent).

title: Internal audit assurance over AI governance using IIA and COSO frameworks
problem: Organisations expect assurance over their AI but internal audit is not ready: only 28% of surveyed leaders were confident in their teams' ability to audit AI risks.
approach: The IIA framework, updated 13 Sep 2024, gives a principles-based structure to assess AI governance maturity, risks and controls.
COSO's February 2026 publication groups GenAI use into eight capability types; EY says add AI systems with ICFR impact to audit scope.
The chief audit executive decides the advisory versus assurance posture.

title: Idea: continuous AI-assisted assurance over AI systems instead of annual audits
problem: Idea, not a deployment: annual audit plans cannot keep pace with continuously changing AI systems, and agents may change behaviour to work around anomalies.
approach: Idea: move to continuous monitoring with real-time dashboards and dynamic audit planning, as discussed at Genpact's CAE Forum.
EY conference speakers said AI can monitor AI performance and detect drift early, starting with simple automations before multi-agent set-ups.
Humans oversee AI-generated outputs and processes.

title: Scope an AI assessment as governance, conformity or performance, and say which
problem: Terms such as assurance, audit, certification and conformity assessment are used interchangeably for different AI assessments, and the variety of approaches is challenging.
approach: The ACCA and EY paper describes three types: governance assessments, conformity assessments against laws and standards, and performance assessments against predefined metrics.
EY recommends each assessment state what is assessed, use clear criteria and be done by a qualified provider.
Practitioners scope, select criteria and give the opinion; scope is negotiated because no comprehensive framework exists.

title: AI governance gap assessment against ISO 42001 and NIST AI RMF
problem: Clients adopting AI need to know where their governance falls short of a benchmark standard before an auditor, certifier or customer asks.
approach: Deloitte UK describes a five-pillar framework aligned to ISO/IEC 42001, with no-regret steps such as a governance committee and AI system inventory.
Deloitte Singapore's June 2026 posting shows staff maintaining client AI risk registers and gap analyses; KPMG Nederland offers readiness scans.
Senior consultants review risk and quality reports.
who: Deloitte UK, Deloitte Singapore, KPMG Nederland

title: Reasonable-assurance opinion over AI governance and controls (SOC 2+ criteria)
problem: Customers and boards cannot see whether a supplier's AI is governed in practice rather than only on paper, and no framework mandates external AI assurance.
approach: KPMG UK combines its Trusted AI framework with SOC principles to give an ISAE (UK) 3000 opinion on AI controls.
KPMG's January 2026 paper calls this SOC 2+; CSA published guidelines in March 2026 for CPAs providing SOC 2+ attestation.
KPMG UK says procurement teams increasingly request AI assurance (self-reported).
who: KPMG UK, KPMG US, CSA, Baker Tilly

title: ISO/IEC 42001 certification of an AI management system by an accredited body
problem: Customers want evidence that an AI developer's governance works but cannot inspect its models directly, and ISO 42001 certifies a management system, not individual AI systems.
approach: A certification body audits the AI management system in two stages, followed by annual surveillance audits over a three-year certificate cycle.
BSI's Umony and Accelleo cases describe certification; Schellman became the first ANAB-accredited body; Anthropic, Sierra and Zendesk posted certificates.
Auditors decide stage 1 and 2 outcomes; accreditation bodies witness certifier audits.

title: Accredit and oversee AI management system certifiers against ISO/IEC 42006
problem: A certificate is only as trustworthy as its issuer, and the AI assurance supplier base is growing faster than accreditation can vet entrants.
approach: ISO/IEC 42006 sets extra requirements, on top of ISO/IEC 17021-1, for bodies that audit and certify AI management systems.
BSI announced ANAB accreditation for ISO/IEC 42001 on 10 Mar 2026, adding to UKAS and RvA, and holds all three (self-reported).
Accreditation bodies assess certifiers' competence, impartiality and consistency, including by witnessing audits.

title: Audit firms certify their own AI management systems before selling AI assurance
problem: A firm selling AI governance advice or assurance must show it holds itself to the same standard, and clients ask who has been through the process.
approach: Firms obtain ISO/IEC 42001 certification from accredited bodies: KPMG US announced 18 Nov 2025 (Schellman); KPMG International followed in December 2025.
SGS certified PwC Taiwan on 15 Jun 2026, and two EY Italian entities hold certificates.
Firms present the certificate as proof of experience (self-reported); a certification-body audit and decision applies.

title: Audit firms build AI assurance service lines, including certification bodies
problem: AI assurance has no clear standards, quality ranges from superficial advice to technical reviews, and many providers are the developers themselves.
approach: June 2025 press reports said the Big Four were positioning to offer AI assurance; EY's 7 Apr 2026 release describes services.
EY Japan names EY CertifyPoint as its certification body; PwC Canada launched an ISO 42001 certification solution on 16 Feb 2026.
Partner sign-off on opinions is not described in the sources.

title: Certify AI agents through adversarial testing, an authorised auditor and insurance (AIUC-1)
problem: Enterprise teams run bespoke risk assessments of AI agents, liability is uncertain, and agent behaviour changes after a point-in-time audit.
approach: AIUC runs technical evaluations with thousands of adversarial scenarios and issues the certificate; Schellman collects audit evidence. Agents are re-tested quarterly.
KPMG LLP's aIQ Capture platform was certified on 27 Aug 2026 after more than 900 technical tests (vendor-published).
The first AIUC-1-backed insurance policy (ElevenLabs) was reported at $50 million of cover (vendor-published).

title: System-level technical assurance of a specific AI system
problem: Governance certification does not tell a buyer whether an individual AI system performs as claimed, and much UK AI assurance comes from developers themselves.
approach: Engagements borrow the financial-audit model: select criteria, then gather evidence by inspection, inquiry, reperformance and analytical testing, as in NYC bias audits.
BSI offers algorithm auditing; Deloitte UK lists third-party challenge over technical build; KPMG Nederland added AI Assurance in Sep 2025.
Practitioners scope, select criteria and give the opinion.
who: BSI, Deloitte UK, KPMG Nederland, Babl AI

title: Mandated independent bias audits of automated hiring tools (New York City)
problem: Employers using automated employment decision tools must obtain annual independent bias audits, but the law leaves auditor and tool loosely defined.
approach: Since July 2023 New York City employers using these tools must undergo annual bias audits by an independent auditor.
An interview study of 16 experts found four auditor roles and concluded the law has not created an effective regime (independent).
The independent auditor signs the bias audit.

title: EU AI Act conformity assessment and compliance assurance for high-risk AI
problem: Providers of high-risk AI systems must show conformity with the Act, but harmonised standards and conformity-assessment capacity are not ready.
approach: Under Article 43, providers choose internal control or notified-body assessment by system type; the first harmonised standard entered enquiry 30 Oct 2025.
The AI Omnibus moved Annex III obligations to 2 Dec 2027.
Deloitte UK offers third-party challenge over compliance, including conformity assessment; the provider or notified body signs off.
who: Deloitte UK, KPMG UK, European Commission

title: Buyers verify AI assurance evidence through certificate registers and trust marks
problem: Procurement teams receive certificates and reports whose meaning depends on who issued them, and two clean SOC 2 reports can cover different control sets.
approach: A five-minute register check of who accredited the certifier and whether the scope is right is recommended for ISO 42001 certificates.
CSA's STAR for AI Level 1 is a self-assessment; Level 2 adds an accredited ISO 42001 certificate; AIUC-1 joined 30 Jun 2026.
Procurement or risk reviewers confirm the scope covers the AI system being bought.
who: Cloud Security Alliance, KPMG UK, techUK

title: Professionalise AI assurers through credentials, competence frameworks and ethics code
problem: The UK government says it is hard to judge existing AI assurance certifications, none issued by UKAS-accredited organisations, and assurers often struggle to get information.
approach: DSIT's Sep 2025 roadmap set four actions, including a professionalisation consortium; techUK says the consortium is drafting an ethics code.
ISACA offers an Advanced in AI Audit certification for holders of qualifying designations such as CISA, CPA or ACA.
Credentials require exams and experience; an accreditation decision by a recognised authority would follow, if introduced.

title: External auditors receive a third-party agent-evaluation attestation as SOX audit input (MSCI)
problem: When an AI agent makes decisions touching SOX systems, auditors ask whether it does what its policy says, and MSCI's CISO said existing documents did not answer that.
approach: MSCI's SecOps Agent approves privileged-access requests; AIUC's red team ran about 1,400 tests, including across 112 privileged roles (vendor-published).
A signed evaluation attestation went to MSCI's external auditors as input to its 2026 SOX audit.
The agent passed with no major or significant vulnerabilities; the external auditors decide how far the report supports their conclusions.

title: Developer-versus-deployer responsibility matrix for scoping AI-agent assurance (AIUC-1)
problem: Agents are built on one platform and run by another organisation, so each side can assume the other covers a control, leaving gaps.
approach: AIUC's 15 Oct 2026 release publishes a template matrix of who typically meets each control across 78 core controls.
AIUC says typically 33 are met by the developer, 40 by the deployer, 5 by the evaluator (vendor-published); no use is reported.
Assurer and client agree the matrix for the specific platform.

title: Idea: CPAs build audit packages so reviewers can verify AI analysis
problem: Idea, not a deployment: AI agents generate analysis far faster than people can check it; the example is mathematics, where peer review takes about a year.
approach: In the maths case, CPA Richie Sater had AI agents answer a 1986 open problem, and sent a mathematician an audit package.
He says the package let reviewers look quickly and was sent to peer review (self-reported); he proposes the same for financial models.
No business client is named; the mathematician reviews the package.
